big_idea: Some events ALWAYS happen, some SOMETIMES happen, some NEVER happen — that's LIKELIHOOD.
learning_intention: We are learning to describe how likely familiar events are to happen.
student_learning_goal: I can tell if events ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, or NEVER happen.
success_criteria: I can name an event that ALWAYS happens.
I can name an event that SOMETIMES happens.
I can name an event that NEVER happens.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Three corner labels (ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, NEVER) — paper signs on classroom walls
Event picture cards (8-10 simple events: sun rises, fish flies, it rains, etc.)
Lesson 4 likelihood tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Detective Dot says: 'Does the sun rise EVERY day? Does a fish FLY every day? Does it rain EVERY day?' Three different answers — that's LIKELIHOOD!
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot + Tally puppets. 'Friends — Detective Dot has THREE new words today. Listen for the difference.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, and NEVER on chart in big letters. 'ALWAYS = every single day. SOMETIMES = some days, not every day. NEVER = no day.'

Demonstrate with three benchmark events:
- 'The sun rises in the morning.' Children think. 'EVERY day? YES — ALWAYS.' Stick to the ALWAYS column.
- 'A fish swims in lava.' Children think. 'EVER? NO — NEVER.' Stick to the NEVER column.
- 'It rains today.' Children think. 'Every day? No. No day? No. SOMETIMES.' Stick to the SOMETIMES column.

More events:
- 'We breathe air.' (ALWAYS — we have to.)
- 'A tree dances.' (NEVER — trees can't dance.)
- 'Lunch is sandwiches.' (SOMETIMES — depends on the day.)
- 'The sky is green.' (NEVER — sky is blue.)
- 'Friday is after Thursday.' (ALWAYS — calendar order.)

Class refrain: 'ALWAYS — SOMETIMES — NEVER — that's LIKELIHOOD!' Chant 3x clapping each word.

Detective Dot's test: 'EVERY day or NO day? If you can't say either, it's SOMETIMES.'

'Today we sort events into ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, or NEVER and write our own.'
student_actions: Listen to Detective Dot's events and call out 'ALWAYS', 'SOMETIMES', or 'NEVER'.
Stand in the matching corner of the room (3 corners labelled).

steps.instruction: WHOLE-GROUP MINI-LESSON (5 min): Detective Dot defines ALWAYS / SOMETIMES / NEVER with three benchmark events: 'we breathe air' (ALWAYS), 'it snows on Tuesday' (SOMETIMES), 'a fish swims in lava' (NEVER). Class chants the refrain.
steps.teacher_prompt: Detective Dot: 'ALWAYS — SOMETIMES — NEVER — that's LIKELIHOOD!'

steps.instruction: STATION A — ALWAYS HAPPENS: 4 children rotate to the ALWAYS corner. Each child names one event that ALWAYS happens (e.g., 'the sun rises'). Teacher records on chart.
steps.teacher_prompt: Detective Dot: 'If it ALWAYS happens, it's CERTAIN.'

steps.instruction: STATION B — SOMETIMES HAPPENS: 4 children rotate to the SOMETIMES corner. Each child names one event that SOMETIMES happens (e.g., 'it rains on Friday').
steps.teacher_prompt: Detective Dot: 'SOMETIMES means it COULD or COULDN'T.'

steps.instruction: STATION C — NEVER HAPPENS: 4 children rotate to the NEVER corner. Each child names one event that NEVER happens (e.g., 'a tree dances').
steps.teacher_prompt: Detective Dot: 'If it NEVER happens, it's IMPOSSIBLE.'

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: Two children share their SOMETIMES events. Class debates: which is more likely? Which is less likely? Cite Fischbein (1975) — likelihood lives on a continuum.
steps.teacher_prompt: Detective Dot: 'SOMETIMES has a SCALE — more likely, less likely.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A (ALWAYS only). Pick from 2-3 sample events instead of generating their own.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station B: rank two SOMETIMES events as more/less likely and explain.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Sentence frame: 'It ___ happens. It is ___.' (filling in always/sometimes/never).
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER PATH: children stand in three corners — ALWAYS corner, SOMETIMES corner, NEVER corner; teacher calls events; children walk to the matching corner and explain why.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: correctly assigns ALWAYS events; correctly assigns NEVER events; correctly assigns SOMETIMES events (not just as catchall).

discussion_prompts: What does SOMETIMES mean? (Some days, not every day.)
What is the test? (EVERY day or NO day? If neither — SOMETIMES.)
consolidation.exit_routine: Detective Dot's refrain — class chants 3x: 'ALWAYS — SOMETIMES — NEVER — that's LIKELIHOOD!' Each child writes one ALWAYS or NEVER event on a sticky.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Likelihood-word use: child correctly assigns ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, NEVER to events and justifies SOMETIMES as 'some days but not every day'.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 4 captures A8.4 — describing how likely familiar events are to happen.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child uses SOMETIMES as a catchall — repairing the uncertainty-collapse trap at K (Fischbein, 1975; Konold, 1989)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On likelihood (A8.4), the most-documented K trap is uncertainty collapse: children commit to neither extreme and assign SOMETIMES to virtually every event, including events that are actually CERTAIN (ALWAYS) or IMPOSSIBLE (NEVER). Fischbein's (1975) intuitive-probability work showed K children resist commitment to 'every day' or 'no day' because they confuse probability with personal uncertainty — 'I don't know if I'll see the sun tomorrow' becomes 'the sun rising is SOMETIMES'. Konold (1989) calls this the 'outcome approach': the child reasons about a single trial, not the long-run pattern.

Why this matters: SOMETIMES is the gateway to Grade 1-3 probability language ('likely', 'unlikely', 'impossible', 'certain'). If K children leave with SOMETIMES = catchall, they lose the contrast that makes the scale meaningful. Sarama & Clements (2009) trajectories place the ALWAYS/NEVER boundary case BEFORE introducing graded uncertainty — secure the absolutes first.

The walkthrough covers when a child says SOMETIMES for an obvious ALWAYS or NEVER event.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station C (NEVER). Detective Dot reads: 'A fish swims in lava.' Child says 'SOMETIMES — maybe a fish could swim in lava sometimes.'
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'Detective Dot has a TEST for SOMETIMES. Ready?'

The test. 'Detective Dot asks two questions. Listen. ONE — does it happen EVERY day? TWO — does it happen on NO day?'

Apply. 'A fish in lava — does that happen EVERY day? No. Does it happen NO day? YES — fish CAN'T swim in lava, lava is hot lava melts fish.'

Generalise. 'NO day = NEVER. The fish in lava is NEVER. Stick it on NEVER.'

The child re-checks. 'Yeah — NEVER.'

Now flip. 'Sun rises tomorrow — does that happen EVERY day? YES. EVERY day = ALWAYS. Stick it on ALWAYS.'

Now contrast. 'It rains tomorrow — does it rain EVERY day? No. NO day? No, it rains some days. SOMETIMES is for IN-BETWEEN. ONLY in-between gets SOMETIMES.'

Long-term recovery: every event MUST pass the EVERY day or NO day test BEFORE being assigned SOMETIMES. Repeat the two-question test for the next 3 events the child meets.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Says SOMETIMES for every event including obvious ALWAYS or NEVER.
(Mid) Sorts ALWAYS and NEVER correctly when prompted with 'EVERY day or NO day?' but defaults to SOMETIMES without the prompt.
(Strong) Self-applies the EVERY day / NO day test and assigns ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, NEVER consistently.
(Stretched) Justifies a SOMETIMES choice by ruling out both extremes ('not every day, not no day, so SOMETIMES').
common_misconceptions: SOMETIMES means 'I'm not sure'. (Repair: SOMETIMES means 'on some days but not every day' — it is about the world, not your knowledge.)
If I have never seen it, it is NEVER. (Repair: NEVER means it CANNOT happen — fish can't fly. Other things you haven't seen, like it snowing in summer somewhere, are SOMETIMES.)
Magical events go in SOMETIMES. (Repair: a tree dancing or pigs flying is NEVER — impossible — not SOMETIMES. Use the 'CAN it happen?' test for NEVER candidates.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child says SOMETIMES for everything: anchor with obvious ALWAYS ('we breathe') and NEVER ('fish flies') examples first; force the 'EVERY day or NO day?' two-question test before any SOMETIMES is allowed.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child swaps ALWAYS and NEVER: drill 'ALWAYS = EVERY day; NEVER = NO day'; act it out — point at calendar (every square = ALWAYS) vs no square = NEVER.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child names but cannot justify: force the sentence frame 'It is ___ because it happens ___' (always / on some days but not every / on no days).

worksheet_brief.purpose: Children sort 8 events into ALWAYS/SOMETIMES/NEVER columns and write one event of their own.
